title: Look and See: spec, spic, vid and vis
short: spec and spic mean look; vid and vis mean see.
trouble: The root also hides inside words that no longer feel like "seeing" words, like auspicious (from watching birds) and specious (from appearance).

blocks.html: Two Latin roots do the looking for English. spec (also spic and spect) means “look”: to inspect is to look into, a spectator looks on. vid (also vis) means “see”: video, vision, evident (easy to see).

blocks.html: Add a prefix and the root tells you which way someone looks. circumspect: looking around. introspective: looking within. retrospect: looking back. provident: seeing ahead. perspicacious: seeing through things.

blocks.title: A word with a story
blocks.q: The sunny morning seemed an auspicious start to the camping trip. What does auspicious mean, and what do birds have to do with it?
steps: Take it apart: au (bird, from Latin avis, as in aviation) + spic (look) + -ious.
In ancient Rome, an official watched the flight of birds and read it as a sign of how a plan would turn out.
A good sign came to be called auspicious. A sunny morning is a good sign for a camping trip.
blocks.a: Showing signs of future success; favorable.

blocks.name: vo-word

entry.def: promising good things to come; favorable
entry.ex: A sunny sky on opening day was an {auspicious} start for the new farmers’ market.
entry.ctx: The team’s first season began on an {auspicious} note: they won their opening three games, and the coach began to hope for a championship.
entry.etym: From Latin auspicium, the reading of signs in the flight of birds, from auspex, “bird watcher”: avis (bird) + specere (to look).

mn.cue: AW, SPECIAL! a rainbow on race day
mn.text: On the morning of the big race, a rainbow arches over the track and Tia gasps, “Aw, special!” A sign that things will go well is {auspicious}.

scene.alt: A runner cheers at a rainbow over the track as a bright bird flies past.

blocks.cap: A word from the list: auspicious.

blocks.name: vo-word

entry.def: seeming true or right at first but false underneath
entry.ex: The ad’s {specious} promise that the shoes would make anyone run faster fooled no one on the track team.
entry.ctx: Dev’s argument sounded convincing at first, but it was {specious}: when his sister checked the numbers, every one of his facts turned out to be wrong.
entry.etym: From Latin speciosus, “good-looking, showy,” from species, “appearance,” from specere (to look). It once meant simply “fair to see.”
entry.note: Specious (only seeming true) is not spacious (roomy); it comes from species, “appearance.”

mn.text: “See? Shush, don’t check!” says the salesman, because his claim only sounds right until someone looks closely. It is {specious}.

scene.alt: A sly salesman hushes a boy who is inspecting his magic beans sign with a magnifying glass.

blocks.cap: A word from the list: specious.

blocks.html: Missing the root when the word no longer feels like a “seeing” word. auspicious comes from watching birds for signs; specious comes from species, “appearance”: a specious argument looks right but is false. Neither is about eyes today, but the root is still there.
